column1: # The passages that tell what happened where (TSK-1235, replacing TSK-1220's whole books).
# A place named with a record in one of these verses is in the "story" group of the record's places;
# a place named with it only elsewhere is folded under the letters and prophecy.
# Story is prose that tells what happened and where: the narrative books, and the narrative episodes
# inside the prophets, Job and the letters. Not story: poems and songs, oracles, laws and commands for
# what is to come, visions, and the greetings of letters, even inside a narrative book. A speech inside
# a narrative book that retells what happened (Moses in Deuteronomy 1-3, Stephen in Acts 7) counts;
# a retelling inside a psalm, an oracle or a letter's argument does not. A letter writer's own account
# of where he was counts (Paul in Galatians 1-2).
# Source: the text itself, read for each range in the KJV's verse numbers, which the canonical frame
# follows; where a poem or oracle starts inside a narrative, the range starts at its first verse.
# Ranges sit on chapters wherever an edition numbers the verses differently (Numbers 30, Daniel 4-6,
# Jonah 1-2). Psalm headings that tell an event (Psalm 60) are not counted, for the same reason.
# Inside the prophets' narrative chapters, an oracle that names places away from the scene is taken
# out verse by verse (Jeremiah 26:4-6, 43:10-13). Inside the narrative books, a prophet's word spoken
# in the scene stays with it (2 Kings 20:17, and Isaiah 36-39, which is the same text) unless it is a
# long oracle of its own (2 Kings 19:21-34); parables and teaching in the Gospels stay with the
# Columns: book (its slug), passage ("all", a chapter, chapters "36-39", verses "23:7-10" or
# "36:1-37:21"), story or not, and why. Rows are read in order and the last row that holds a verse
# decides; a book without a row tells no story.
